claims.evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of ZCWPW1 CUT&RUN data with published SPO11-oligo data.

claims.claim: ZCWPW1 signal exhibits positive correlation with SPO11-oligo density, DMC1-SSDS and PRDM9 binding signals.
claims.source: Additionally, ZCWPW1 signal exhibits positive correlation with SPO11-oligo density, DMC1-SSDS and PRDM9 binding signals (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis of ZCWPW1 signal with other recombination metrics.

claims.claim: PRDM9 binding generates a nucleosome-depleted region with nucleosomes organized symmetrically around PRDM9 binding sites.
claims.source: PRDM9 binding generates a nucleosome-depleted region with nucleosomes organized symmetrically around PRDM9 binding sites (Baker et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claims.claim: Only 8%, 9% and 5% of ZCWPW1 called peaks overlap with TSS, TES and CGI respectively.
claims.source: Next, we looked for ZCWPW1 overlap with functional regions in the genome: Transcription Start Sites (TSS), Transcription End Sites (TES) and CpG islands (CGI), and we found only 8%, 9% and 5% of our ZCWPW1 called peaks overlap with these sites respectively (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by genomic overlap analysis of ZCWPW1 peaks.

claims.claim: There was no significant ZCWPW1 enrichment genome-wide at TSS, TES, and CGI compared to IgG control.
claims.source: Despite ZCWPW1 peaks overlapping with these sites, there was no significant ZCWPW1 enrichment genome-wide in these functional sites compared to IgG control (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 3C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of ZCWPW1 signal to IgG control at functional genomic sites.

claims.claim: 85% of ZCWPW1 peaks overlapped with regions containing both H3K4me3 and H3K36me3 marks.
claims.source: The vast majority of ZCWPW1 peaks overlapped with regions containing both H3K4me3 and H3K36me3 marks (85%), with significantly less peaks overlapping with regions marked by either mark alone (Figure 3C, Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by overlap analysis of ZCWPW1 peaks with histone modification ChIP-seq data.

claims.claim: ZCWPW1 CUT&RUN signals are significantly stronger in peaks with H3K4me3/H3K36me3 dual marks compared to regions with a single mark.
claims.source: In agreement with in vitro binding assays (Figure 1D, Figure 1E), we found that ZCWPW1 CUT&RUN signals are significantly stronger in peaks with H3K4me3/H3K36me3 dual marks compared to regions with a single mark (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of ZCWPW1 signal strength at different histone modification states.

claims.claim: No enrichment of ZCWPW1 relative to control was observed in the pseudo-autosomal region (PAR) of sex chromosomes.
claims.source: Finally, we did not observe any enrichment of ZCWPW1 relative to control in the pseudo-autosomal region (PAR) of sex chromosomes, which undergoes PRDM9-independent recombination in mice (Brick et al., 2012; Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of ZCWPW1 signal at PAR region compared to control.

claims.claim: Motif analysis identified exclusively the PRDM9 binding motif of the Dom2 allele (PRDM9Dom2) within ZCWPW1 peak regions (p=1e-261).
claims.source: This analysis identified exclusively the PRDM9 binding motif of the Dom2 allele (PRDM9Dom2), found within the C57Bl/6J strain (p=1e-261) (Figure 4—source data 1), suggesting that ZCWPW1 occupancy is solely PRDM9-dependent.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by de novo motif discovery analysis of ZCWPW1 peaks.

claims.claim: 8,976 ZCWPW1 peaks were identified in F1-hybrid mouse spermatocytes from a C57Bl/6J (B6) and CAST/EiJ (CAST) cross.
claims.source: In these mice, we identified 8,976 peaks, 60% of which overlap with previously described CAST/CAST hotspots (Smagulova et al., 2016), while only 18% overlap with B6/B6 hotspots (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), a finding consistent with reported PRDM9Cast dominance in hybrid mice (Baker et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by CUT&RUN data from F1-hybrid mice.

claims.claim: 60% of ZCWPW1 peaks in F1-hybrid mice overlap with previously described CAST/CAST hotspots.
claims.source: In these mice, we identified 8,976 peaks, 60% of which overlap with previously described CAST/CAST hotspots (Smagulova et al., 2016), while only 18% overlap with B6/B6 hotspots (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), a finding consistent with reported PRDM9Cast dominance in hybrid mice (Baker et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by overlap analysis of ZCWPW1 peaks with published hotspot data.

claims.claim: 18% of ZCWPW1 peaks in F1-hybrid mice overlap with B6/B6 hotspots.
claims.source: In these mice, we identified 8,976 peaks, 60% of which overlap with previously described CAST/CAST hotspots (Smagulova et al., 2016), while only 18% overlap with B6/B6 hotspots (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), a finding consistent with reported PRDM9Cast dominance in hybrid mice (Baker et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by overlap analysis of ZCWPW1 peaks with published hotspot data.

claims.claim: ZCWPW1 binds to 1,383 novel hotspots that do not exist in either B6/B6 or CAST/CAST mice, but only appear in F1-hybrids.
claims.source: Furthermore, ZCWPW1 also binds to 1,383 novel hotspots that do not exist in either B6/B6 or CAST/CAST mice, but only appear in F1-hybrids, where PRDM9Cast binds to the B6 genome and PRDM9Dom2 binds to the CAST genome (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of ZCWPW1 peaks unique to F1-hybrid mice.

claims.claim: De novo motif discovery in the hybrids revealed two motifs identical to PRDM9Cast and PRDM9Dom2 (p=1e-768 and 1e-60 respectively).
claims.source: De novo motif discovery in the hybrids revealed two motifs identical to PRDM9Cast and PRDM9Dom2 (p=1e-768 and 1e-60 respectively) (Figure 4A; Figure 4—source data 2).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by de novo motif discovery analysis of ZCWPW1 peaks in F1-hybrid mice.

claims.claim: ZCWPW1 occupancy is a novel marker for meiotic hotspots that reflects PRDM9 allele specificity.
claims.source: Overall, these results indicate that ZCWPW1 occupancy is a novel marker for meiotic hotspots that reflects PRDM9 allele specificity, and ZCWPW1 CUT&RUN is a useful method to infer PRDM9 binding sites.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the allele-specific binding patterns of ZCWPW1.

claims.claim: Zcwpw1 KO mice were born healthy and at mendelian ratios.
claims.source: To test that hypothesis, we generated mice with homozygous deletion of Zcwpw1 (Zcwpw1 KO), which were born healthy and at mendelian ratios.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on observation of Zcwpw1 KO mice.

claims.claim: Zcwpw1 KO testes are smaller and have reduced mass (80 mg vs.190 mg) compared to wild type.
claims.source: Western blotting confirmed the absence of ZCWPW1 in testis from Zcwpw1 KO mice (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), which are smaller and have reduced mass (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B) compared to wild type (Zcwpw1 WT) (80 mg vs.190 mg).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by measurement of testis mass in WT and KO mice.

claims.claim: Zcwpw1 KO testes show total absence of spermatids in the seminiferous tubules.
claims.source: Hematoxylin and Eosin (H&E) staining of tissue sections demonstrated the total absence of spermatids in the seminiferous tubules of Zcwpw1 KO testes (Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by histological analysis of testis sections.

claims.claim: Zcwpw1 KO mice arrest at a pachytene-like stage of prophase I.
claims.source: SYCP3/SYCP1 staining revealed that Zcwpw1 KO mice arrest at a pachytene-like stage of prophase I (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence staining of spermatocyte spreads.

claims.claim: Almost all spermatocytes in Zcwpw1 KO mice displayed partial chromosomal asynapsis.
claims.source: In Zcwpw1 KO mice, almost all spermatocytes displayed partial chromosomal asynapsis (Figure 5C), with an average of 12 autosomal chromosomes synapsed per spermatocyte (out of 19), in contrast to Zcwpw1 WT spermatocytes which -with rare exceptions- have all homologous autosomal chromosomes fully synapsed in spermatocytes at the pachytene stage (Figure 5D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of synapsed chromosomes in spermatocyte spreads.

claims.claim: Zcwpw1 KO spermatocytes have an average of 12 autosomal chromosomes synapsed per spermatocyte (out of 19).
claims.source: In Zcwpw1 KO mice, almost all spermatocytes displayed partial chromosomal asynapsis (Figure 5C), with an average of 12 autosomal chromosomes synapsed per spermatocyte (out of 19), in contrast to Zcwpw1 WT spermatocytes which -with rare exceptions- have all homologous autosomal chromosomes fully synapsed in spermatocytes at the pachytene stage (Figure 5D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of synapsed chromosomes in spermatocyte spreads.

claims.claim: Spermatocytes from Zcwpw1 KO mice have widespread focal accumulation of DMC1 in the cells arrested at pachytene-like stage.
claims.source: Spermatocytes from Zcwpw1 KO mice have widespread focal accumulation of DMC1 in the cells arrested at pachytene-like stage (Figure 5E), with significantly increased numbers of DMC1 foci per spermatocyte in Zcwpw1 KO (Figure 5F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence staining and quantification of DMC1 foci.

claims.claim: Zcwpw1 KO spermatocytes have significantly increased numbers of DMC1 foci per spermatocyte.
claims.source: Spermatocytes from Zcwpw1 KO mice have widespread focal accumulation of DMC1 in the cells arrested at pachytene-like stage (Figure 5E), with significantly increased numbers of DMC1 foci per spermatocyte in Zcwpw1 KO (Figure 5F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of DMC1 foci in spermatocyte spreads.

claims.claim: γ-H2AX staining showed significant accumulation on autosomes and the absence of the XY sex body in Zcwpw1 KO spermatocytes.
claims.source: Furthermore, γ-H2AX staining showed significant accumulation on autosomes and the absence of the XY sex body, indicating prophase blockage before sex body formation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence staining of spermatocyte spreads.

claims.claim: Zcwpw1 KO spermatocytes have pachytene-like meiotic arrest with partial asynapsis and increased DMC1 foci compared to Zcwpw1 WT spermatocytes.
claims.source: Our observations from immunofluorescence staining are in agreement with what has been recently reported by two different groups who found that Zcwpw1 KO spermatocytes have pachytene-like meiotic arrest with partial asynapsis and increased DMC1 foci compared to Zcwpw1 WT spermatocytes (Li et al., 2019a; Wells et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' data and citations to other published studies.

claims.claim: Zcwpw1 KO mice phenocopy Prdm9 null male mice in which sperm production is compromised by partially defective DSB repair and synapsis with meiotic arrest at a pachytene-like stage.
claims.source: Collectively, Zcwpw1 KO mice phenocopy Prdm9 null male mice in which sperm production is compromised by partially defective DSB repair and synapsis with meiotic arrest at a pachytene-like stage (Brick et al., 2012; Hayashi et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on comparison of Zcwpw1 KO phenotype with published Prdm9 KO phenotype.

claims.claim: In Prdm9-null male mice, meiotic DSBs reposition away from PRDM9 bound motifs to promoters and at other sites of PRDM9-independent H3K4me3.
claims.source: In Prdm9-null male mice, meiotic DSBs reposition away from PRDM9 bound motifs to promoters and at other sites of PRDM9-independent H3K4me3 (Brick et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claims.claim: END-seq identified 2,098 and 3,147 DSB sites in spermatocytes from Zcwpw1 WT and Zcwpw1 KO mice respectively.
claims.source: Peak calling on END-seq reads identified 2,098 and 3,147 DSB sites in spermatocytes from Zcwpw1 WT and Zcwpw1 KO mice respectively.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by END-seq data and peak calling analysis.

claims.claim: DSBs in Zcwpw1 KO mice nearly completely overlapped with DSBs in Zcwpw1 WT.
claims.source: Surprisingly, unlike the case in Prdm9 KO, DSBs in Zcwpw1 KO mice nearly completely overlapped with DSBs in Zcwpw1 WT, and with previously identified hotpots in B6 mice using DMC1 SSDS (Figure 6A, Figure 6B, Figure 6C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by overlap analysis of END-seq peaks between WT and KO.

claims.claim: Unlike in Prdm9 KO mice, DSBs in Zcwpw1 KO were not repositioned towards promoters.
claims.source: Importantly, unlike in Prdm9 KO mice, DSBs were not repositioned towards promoters (Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by END-seq data showing DSB distribution at promoters.

claims.claim: ZCWPW1 is not required for the positioning of DSBs, rather it is required exclusively for efficient DSB repair and homologous recombination.
claims.source: In sum these data indicate that unlike PRDM9, ZCWPW1 is not required for the positioning of DSBs, rather it is required exclusively for efficient DSB repair and homologous recombination.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the END-seq data showing DSB positioning is unchanged in Zcwpw1 KO.

claims.claim: PRDM9 is a unique SET domain containing histone methyltransferase that contains its own specific DNA binding domain, a rapidly evolving C2H2 zinc finger array.
claims.source: PRDM9 is a unique SET domain containing histone methyltransferase in several respects. First, it contains its own specific DNA binding domain, a rapidly evolving C2H2 zinc finger array that binds to target sequences with high specificity.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about PRDM9 structure and function.

claims.claim: PRDM9 contains a dual specificity histone methyltransferase activity for histone H3 K4 and histone H3 K36.
claims.source: Second, it contains a dual specificity histone methyltransferase activity for histone H3 K4 and histone H3 K36 (Eram et al., 2014; Powers et al., 2016; Wu et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claims.claim: ZCWPW1 is a unique protein that possesses dual histone methylation reader domains; a zf-CW domain that binds to the H3K4me3 mark, and a PWWP domain that binds to the H3K36me3 mark.
claims.source: Likewise, ZCWPW1 is a unique protein that possesses dual histone methylation reader domains; a zf-CW domain that has previously been shown to bind to the H3K4me3 mark (He et al., 2010), and a PWWP domain, which has been shown on multiple proteins including DNMT3a and DNMT3b to bind to the H3K36me3 mark (Rondelet et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature about domain functions.

claims.claim: ZCWPW1 can bind to histone H3 peptides with double H3K4me3 and H3K36me3 marks in vitro with high affinity at a 1:1 ratio.
claims.source: ZCWPW1 can bind to histone H3 peptides with double H3K4me3 and H3K36me3 marks in vitro with high affinity at a 1:1 ratio.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro binding assays and ITC measurements.

claims.claim: PRDM9 predominantly methylates H3K4me3 and H3K36me3 on the +1, +2,–1 and –2 nucleosomes flanking its binding sites.
claims.source: Furthermore, PRDM9 predominantly methylates H3K4me3 and H3K36me3 on the +1, +2,–1 and –2 nucleosomes flanking its binding sites, which provides a short platform for ZCWPW1 interaction with chromatin at sites in vivo.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about PRDM9 activity and inference about ZCWPW1 binding.

claims.claim: ZCWPW1 is dispensable for initiating DSBs at PRDM9-bound hotspots.
claims.source: Against our expectations, ZCWPW1 is dispensable for initiating DSBs at PRDM9-bound hotspots, as DSBs in Zcwpw1 KO male mice are still located at PRDM9 bound sites.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by END-seq data showing DSB positioning is unchanged in Zcwpw1 KO.

claims.claim: ZCWPW1 is critical for the efficient repair of PRDM9-dependent breaks.
claims.source: Our data instead suggests that ZCWPW1 is critical for the efficient repair of these PRDM9-dependent breaks.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the accumulation of DSB markers in Zcwpw1 KO mice.

claims.claim: PRDM9 histone methyltransferase activity is essential for DSB formation at PRDM9 binding sites.
claims.source: The findings that PRDM9 histone methyltransferase activity is essential for DSB formation at PRDM9 binding sites (Diagouraga et al., 2018; Powers et al., 2016) would therefore seem to suggest that a yet to be described PRDM9 histone methyl reader may link PRDM9 to the DSB machinery upstream of ZCWPW1.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature and speculation about an unknown reader.

claims.claim: ZCWPW2, a paralog of ZCWPW1 that diverged early in evolution, is a possible candidate for linking PRDM9 to the DSB machinery.
claims.source: ZCWPW2, a paralog of ZCWPW1 that diverged early in evolution, is a possible candidate.
claims.evidence: The claim is speculative based on evolutionary relationship between ZCWPW1 and ZCWPW2.

claims.claim: In Zcwpw1 KO spermatocytes, the END-seq profile at hotspots demonstrates the presence of a central peak comparable to WT mice.
claims.source: In Zcwpw1 KO spermatocytes, the END-seq profile at hotspots demonstrates the presence of a central peak comparable to WT mice.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by END-seq data analysis.

claims.claim: Central peaks in END-seq are lost in Dmc1 KO mice which fail to undergo strand invasion.
claims.source: Such central peaks are lost in Dmc1 KO mice which fail to undergo strand invasion (Paiano et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claims.claim: ZCWPW1 functions as a PRDM9 specific synapsis factor that is necessary to bind both the cut and uncut homologs to link PRDM9-bound DNA loops to the SC, to facilitate later steps in meiotic recombination.
claims.source: We propose a model in which ZCWPW1 functions as a PRDM9 specific synapsis factor that is necessary to bind both the cut and uncut homologs to link PRDM9-bound DNA loops to the SC, to facilitate later steps in meiotic recombination.
claims.evidence: The claim is a proposed model based on the data presented.

claims.claim: Symmetrical PRDM9 binding is critical for meiotic recombination.
claims.source: This model is supported by a recent study which suggested that symmetrical PRDM9 binding is critical for meiotic recombination.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by reference to a recent study.

claims.claim: The moderately conserved SCP1 domain found at the N-terminus of mouse ZCWPW1 shares homology to a region of the central axis protein SYCP1 that makes a coiled-coil and facilitates dimerization.
claims.source: A hint may lie within the moderately conserved SCP1 domain found at the N-terminus of mouse ZCWPW1 which shares homology to a region of the central axis protein SYCP1 that makes a coiled-coil and facilitates dimerization (Seo et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on sequence homology and citation to published literature about SYCP1 function.

claims.claim: PRDM9 bound loops could be directly tethered to the SC via ZCWPW1.
claims.source: Thus, PRDM9 bound loops could be directly tethered to the SC via ZCWPW1.
claims.evidence: The claim is speculative based on the SCP1 domain homology.

claims.claim: END-seq is a method of directly sequencing DSBs that can be applied to a single mouse testis to map thousands of hotspots.
claims.source: END-seq is a method of directly sequencing DSBs, and we have applied it to a single mouse testis to map thousands of hotspots.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on the application of END-seq method in this study.

claims.claim: ZCWPW1 CUT&RUN maps mouse hotspots by mapping the occupancy of ZCWPW1 that is directly downstream of PRDM9-induced histone methylation marks.
claims.source: ZCWPW1 CUT&RUN also maps mouse hotspots, by mapping the occupancy of the factor ZCWPW1 that is directly downstream of PRDM9-induced histone methylation marks using a polyclonal antibody.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on the application of ZCWPW1 CUT&RUN method in this study.

claims.claim: ZCWPW1 occupancy correlates positively with the strength of hotspots in mice.
claims.source: Importantly, ZCWPW1 occupancy correlates positively with the strength of hotspots in mice.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis of ZCWPW1 signal with hotspot metrics.

claims.claim: ZCWPW1 CUT&RUN was applied to 300,000 bulk testicular cells from adult mice to sensitively map thousands of mouse hotspots.
claims.source: We applied ZCWPW1 CUT&RUN to 300,000 bulk testicular cells from adult mice (a tiny fraction of the material obtained from a single adult testis) to sensitively map thousands of mouse hotspots.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on the application of ZCWPW1 CUT&RUN method in this study.

claims.claim: In yeast, plants and at least some vertebrates (those that lost PRDM9 like canids and birds), meiotic hotspots are located in the nucleosome free regions at gene promoters.
claims.source: In yeast, plants and at least some vertebrates (those that lost PRDM9 like canids and birds); meiotic hotspots are located in the nucleosome free regions at gene promoters.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge from the literature.

claims.claim: Within species that evolved PRDM9, hotspots are specified by the DNA binding activity of the PRDM9 zinc finger array.
claims.source: However, within species that evolved PRDM9, hotspots are specified by the DNA binding activity of the PRDM9 zinc finger array.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge from the literature.

claims.claim: The emergence of PRDM9 was a landmark that re-shaped patterns of meiotic recombination during evolution.
claims.source: Therefore, the emergence of PRDM9 was a landmark that re-shaped patterns of meiotic recombination during evolution.
claims.evidence: The claim is an inference based on the evolutionary analysis and functional data.

claims.claim: The PRDM9-derived pattern of hotspot selection provided more flexibility in hotspot evolution compared to the ancestral, fixed pattern of hotspots found at promoters and within genes by decoupling hotspot selection away from functional genetic elements.
claims.source: The PRDM9-derived pattern of hotspot selection provided more flexibility in hotspot evolution compared to the ancestral, fixed pattern of hotspots found at promoters and within genes by decoupling hotspot selection away from functional genetic elements.
claims.evidence: The claim is an inference based on the evolutionary analysis and comparison of hotspot patterns.

claims.claim: A histone writer/reader system evolved by co-emergence of PRDM9 (which catalyzes formation of H3K4me3 and H3K36me3 dual marks) and ZCWPW1 (which recognizes these dual marks to facilitate DSB repair at the PRDM9 bound sites).
claims.source: This system evolved by co-emergence of (i) a histone writer (PRDM9) which catalyzes formation of H3K4me3 and H3K36me3 dual marks and (ii) a histone methylation reader (ZCWPW1) which recognizes these dual marks to facilitate DSB repair at the PRDM9 bound sites.
claims.evidence: The claim is an inference based on the functional and evolutionary data presented.

claims.claim: The presence of PRDM9 and ZCWPW1 is crucial for hotspot selection and successful meiotic recombination in mice.
claims.source: The presence of these two factors is crucial for hotspot selection and successful meiotic recombination in mice.
claims.evidence: The claim is an inference based on the functional data showing both factors are required for proper meiosis.

claims.claim: Meiotic crossovers result from homology-directed repair of DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs).
claims.source: Meiotic crossovers result from homology-directed repair of DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge in the field.

claims.claim: In yeast and plants, DSBs are generated near gene promoters.
claims.source: Unlike yeast and plants, where DSBs are generated near gene promoters, in many vertebrates DSBs are enriched at hotspots determined by the DNA binding activity of the rapidly evolving zinc finger array of PRDM9 (PR domain zinc finger protein 9).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge from the literature.

claims.claim: In many vertebrates, DSBs are enriched at hotspots determined by the DNA binding activity of the rapidly evolving zinc finger array of PRDM9.

claims.claim: ZCWPW1 is tightly co-expressed during spermatogenesis with Prdm9.
claims.source: Here, we identify the dual histone methylation reader ZCWPW1, which is tightly co-expressed during spermatogenesis with Prdm9, as an essential meiotic recombination factor required for efficient repair of PRDM9-dependent DSBs and for pairing of homologous chromosomes in male mice.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by single-cell co-expression analysis.

claims.claim: ZCWPW1 is an essential meiotic recombination factor required for efficient repair of PRDM9-dependent DSBs in male mice.

claims.claim: ZCWPW1 is required for pairing of homologous chromosomes in male mice.

claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the asynapsis phenotype observed in Zcwpw1 KO mice.

claims.claim: The evolution of a dual histone methylation writer/reader (PRDM9/ZCWPW1) system in vertebrates remodeled genetic recombination hotspot selection from an ancestral static pattern near genes towards a flexible pattern controlled by the rapidly evolving DNA binding activity of PRDM9.
claims.source: In sum, our results indicate that the evolution of a dual histone methylation writer/reader (PRDM9/ZCWPW1) system in vertebrates remodeled genetic recombination hotspot selection from an ancestral static pattern near genes towards a flexible pattern controlled by the rapidly evolving DNA binding activity of PRDM9.
claims.evidence: The claim is an inference based on the evolutionary and functional data presented.

results.result: ZCWPW1 is highly co-expressed with PRDM9 during spermatogenesis and shows testis-specific expression in both mouse and human.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C3 and C86 provide converging evidence from single-cell RNA-seq correlation analysis (C1), tissue expression profiling (C2-C3), and direct statement of co-expression (C86). The data includes statistical significance (rho=0.519, p=2E-6) and protein-level validation by Western blot.

results.result: ZCWPW1 contains three functional domains (SCP1, zf-CW, PWWP) with varying degrees of conservation across species, where zf-CW and PWWP domains are highly conserved while the SCP1 domain shows weaker conservation.
results.evaluation: Claims C4-C9 and C18-C20 collectively establish the domain architecture through bioinformatics analysis and literature citations. The conservation analysis (C18-C20) is supported by multiple sequence alignment data showing high conservation of zf-CW and PWWP domains and moderate conservation of the SCP1 domain (30% identity with SYCP1).

results.result: ZCWPW1 binds preferentially to dual-modified H3K4me3/K36me3 histone peptides with high affinity (KD = 1.7 ± 0.3 µM) in a 1:1 stoichiometry, showing stronger binding than to single modifications.
results.evaluation: Claims C10-C12 and C60 are supported by two independent in vitro binding assays: biotin-streptavidin pulldown (C10-C11) and isothermal titration calorimetry (C12). The ITC provides quantitative binding affinity measurements with error estimates, demonstrating dual-mark specificity with KD values >10 µM for single marks versus 1.7 µM for dual marks.

results.result: ZCWPW1 functions as a dual histone methylation reader specific for PRDM9-catalyzed marks, with complementary roles in meiosis.
results.evaluation: Claims C13 and C59 are supported by the binding data (C10-C12), domain analysis (C4-C6), and co-expression patterns (C1-C3). The inference that ZCWPW1 is a meiosis-specific reader for PRDM9 marks is well-justified by the convergence of biochemical, structural, and expression data.

results.result: PRDM9 and ZCWPW1 show correlated evolutionary patterns, with both genes lost in birds and crocodiles, and species retaining both genes maintaining all three catalytic tyrosines in PRDM9.
results.evaluation: Claims C14-C15 and C21-C23 are supported by comparative genomic analysis across vertebrate species. The striking correlation (C23) that all species with both genes maintain the three catalytic tyrosines, while only 3/29 species lacking ZCWPW1 maintain them, provides strong evidence for co-evolution. The data is based on systematic database searches and sequence analysis.

results.result: 193 vertebrate species with ZCWPW1 orthologs were identified through database searches and BLAST analysis.
results.evaluation: Claims C16-C17 describe the identification of 174 species from databases and 19 additional species via BLAST, totaling 193 species. The methodology is clearly described with appropriate validation steps including motif analysis and phylogenetic tree construction to distinguish ZCWPW1 from ZCWPW2.

results.result: ZCWPW1 binds to 4,487 genomic sites that overlap extensively with meiotic DSB hotspots (89% with DMC1 sites, 58% with SPO11-oligos) and correlates positively with recombination metrics.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C27 are supported by CUT&RUN sequencing data with appropriate peak calling (p<0.001) and overlap analysis with published datasets. The positive correlation with multiple independent recombination metrics (SPO11-oligo density, DMC1-SSDS, PRDM9 binding) strengthens the conclusion.

results.result: ZCWPW1 shows minimal overlap and no significant enrichment at transcription start sites, transcription end sites, and CpG islands compared to control.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C30 are supported by genomic overlap analysis showing only 5-9% of peaks at these functional sites and comparison to IgG control showing no significant enrichment. This demonstrates specificity for hotspots rather than general promoter/CGI binding.

results.result: 85% of ZCWPW1 peaks overlap with regions containing both H3K4me3 and H3K36me3 marks, with significantly stronger ZCWPW1 signals at dual-marked regions compared to single-marked regions.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C32 are supported by overlap analysis with published ChIP-seq data for H3K4me3 and H3K36me3 in prophase I spermatocytes. The quantitative comparison of signal strength at different modification states is consistent with the in vitro binding data (C10-C12), providing in vivo validation.

results.result: ZCWPW1 shows no enrichment at the pseudo-autosomal region (PAR) of sex chromosomes, which undergoes PRDM9-independent recombination.
results.evaluation: Claim C33 is supported by analysis of ZCWPW1 signal at the PAR region compared to control, demonstrating specificity for PRDM9-dependent hotspots. This negative control strengthens the conclusion that ZCWPW1 binding is PRDM9-dependent.

results.result: ZCWPW1 occupancy is determined by PRDM9 in an allele-specific manner, as demonstrated by motif analysis identifying PRDM9Dom2 and PRDM9Cast motifs in B6 and F1-hybrid mice respectively.
results.evaluation: Claims C34, C39, and C40 are supported by de novo motif discovery analysis showing exclusive identification of PRDM9 binding motifs (p=1e-261 for Dom2, p=1e-768 and 1e-60 for Cast motifs in hybrids). The allele-specific binding pattern in F1-hybrids provides strong evidence for PRDM9-dependent recruitment.

results.result: In F1-hybrid mice, ZCWPW1 binds to 8,976 sites with allele-specific distribution (60% CAST hotspots, 18% B6 hotspots) and identifies 1,383 novel hybrid-specific hotspots.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C38 are supported by CUT&RUN data from F1-hybrid mice with overlap analysis against published hotspot datasets. The PRDM9Cast dominance (60% vs 18%) is consistent with published literature (Baker et al., 2015), and the identification of hybrid-specific hotspots aligns with known PRDM9 binding-site erosion patterns.

results.result: Zcwpw1 KO mice are born healthy but males show azoospermia with reduced testis mass (80 mg vs 190 mg), absence of spermatids, and arrest at pachytene-like stage with partial asynapsis (average 12/19 autosomes synapsed).
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C46 are supported by multiple complementary approaches: Western blot confirmation of knockout, testis mass measurements, H&E histology, and SYCP3/SYCP1 immunofluorescence with quantification. The phenotypic characterization is thorough with appropriate quantification (n=127 cells counted for synapsis analysis).

results.result: Zcwpw1 KO spermatocytes show widespread accumulation of DMC1 foci with significantly increased numbers per cell, and γ-H2AX accumulation on autosomes without XY sex body formation.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C49 are supported by immunofluorescence staining and quantification of DMC1 foci across different meiotic stages. The statistical significance is demonstrated (p-value shown in Figure 5F), and the absence of sex body formation indicates arrest before this stage. These findings suggest intact DSB formation but defective repair.

results.result: The Zcwpw1 KO phenotype (pachytene-like arrest, partial asynapsis, increased DMC1 foci) is consistent with independent reports and phenocopies Prdm9 null mice.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C51 are supported by the authors' data (C42-C49) and citations to two independent studies (Li et al., 2019a; Wells et al., 2019) reporting similar phenotypes. The comparison to Prdm9 KO is supported by literature citations (Brick et al., 2012; Hayashi et al., 2005).

results.result: END-seq analysis reveals that DSBs in Zcwpw1 KO mice (3,147 sites) nearly completely overlap with WT DSBs (2,098 sites) and are not repositioned to promoters, indicating ZCWPW1 is dispensable for DSB positioning but required for efficient repair.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C56 and C62 are supported by END-seq data with spike-in normalization and peak calling. The overlap analysis and comparison to Prdm9 KO (where DSBs reposition to promoters) provides strong evidence that ZCWPW1 functions downstream of DSB formation. The conclusion is well-supported by the data showing maintained DSB positioning despite repair defects.

results.result: ZCWPW1 is critical for efficient DSB repair, with END-seq profiles showing central peaks comparable to WT (unlike Dmc1 KO), suggesting repair defects occur downstream of strand invasion.
results.evaluation: Claims C63, C66, and C67 present a model for ZCWPW1 function based on END-seq peak profiles. While the presence of central peaks (C66) and comparison to Dmc1 KO (C67) are data-supported, the authors acknowledge uncertainty about whether ZCWPW1 acts upstream or downstream of strand invasion due to the heterogeneous cell population and partial asynapsis. The conclusion requires additional experiments to definitively establish the mechanistic step.

results.result: A proposed model suggests ZCWPW1 functions as a PRDM9-specific synapsis factor linking DNA loops to the synaptonemal complex, potentially through the SCP1 domain's homology to SYCP1's dimerization region.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C71 present a speculative model based on the SCP1 domain homology (C70, 30% identity with SYCP1) and functional data. While the model is consistent with the data (asynapsis phenotype, PRDM9-dependent binding, symmetric binding importance), it remains speculative without direct evidence of SC interactions or SCP1 domain function. The authors appropriately acknowledge this as a proposed model requiring further investigation.

results.result: Two novel methods for mapping meiotic hotspots were developed: END-seq (direct DSB sequencing from single testis) and ZCWPW1 CUT&RUN (using 300,000 cells), with ZCWPW1 occupancy correlating positively with hotspot strength.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C75 are supported by the successful application of both methods in this study. END-seq identified thousands of hotspots from single testis (C53), and ZCWPW1 CUT&RUN identified 4,487 peaks from 300,000 cells (C24). The correlation with hotspot strength (C74) is demonstrated in Figure 3—figure supplement 2. Both methods show advantages over existing approaches in terms of material requirements.

results.result: The evolution of the PRDM9/ZCWPW1 dual histone writer/reader system remodeled meiotic recombination hotspot selection from a static promoter-based pattern to a flexible PRDM9-controlled pattern, decoupling hotspot selection from functional genetic elements.
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C81 and C89 present an evolutionary synthesis supported by multiple lines of evidence: co-evolution patterns (C23), functional data showing both factors are required for proper meiosis (C42-C56), and comparison to ancestral systems (C76-C77, C95-C96). The inference is well-justified by the convergence of evolutionary, biochemical, and functional data, though it remains an interpretive framework rather than directly testable.

results.result: PRDM9 histone methyltransferase activity is essential for DSB formation, suggesting an unknown histone methyl reader may link PRDM9 to DSB machinery upstream of ZCWPW1, with ZCWPW2 as a possible candidate.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C65 are speculative. While C64 is supported by literature citations (Diagouraga et al., 2018; Powers et al., 2016), the suggestion of an unknown reader and ZCWPW2 as a candidate (C65) is purely speculative without supporting data. This represents a hypothesis for future investigation rather than a supported result.

results.result: Zcwpw1 KO females show initial fertility with age-related ovarian insufficiency, contrasting with complete infertility in Prdm9 KO females, suggesting PRDM9 has ZCWPW1-independent functions in females.
results.evaluation: Claims C121-C123 are supported by citation to published work (Li et al., 2019a) for the Zcwpw1 KO female phenotype and established literature (Hayashi et al., 2005) for Prdm9 KO females. The inference of ZCWPW1-independent PRDM9 function (C123) is reasonable based on the phenotypic differences, though it requires further investigation.
